sentences: A polynomial-size Boolean circuit represents an efficient nonuniform computation, but its longest chain of dependent gates can be large.
The question asks whether every such computation can be reorganized into logarithmic depth while retaining polynomial size.
Logarithmic depth would permit much greater parallelism without allowing an excessive number of gates.
Counting arguments and restricted circuit lower bounds do not settle this comparison for unrestricted Boolean circuits.
Resolving it would determine whether polynomial-size circuits and the nonuniform version of NC1 have the same expressive power.

cards.title: Six possibilities for locally sampled uniform symmetric distributions
cards.formal: Resolved affirmatively: there exists an absolute constant C such that, for every fixed locality d and ε∈(0,1), all sufficiently large n have the following property. If a d-local Boolean map on independent uniform input bits has output distribution X at total variation distance at most ε from a distribution uniform on a nonempty union of Hamming-weight layers in {0,1}ⁿ, then X is within Cε of one of the six distributions defined below.
cards.why: Classifies the ability of constant-locality classical circuits to generate uniform symmetric distributions, including approximate generation rather than only exact sampling.
cards.status_note: Resolved by Kane, Ostuni and Wu, published at STOC 2025. The complete theorem, locality and distance conventions, absolute constant, threshold dependence and six distributions were checked against arXiv v2. This is published-theorem/model verification, not independent proof verification.

progress.text: The source conjectures the six-distribution classification and proves partial cases for supports concentrated on sublinear Hamming weights.
The STOC paper proves the complete classification, with an approximation constant independent of locality.

cards.definitions: For m,n≥1, a map f:{0,1}ᵐ→{0,1}ⁿ is d-local if each output coordinate depends on at most d input coordinates; the chosen inputs may differ between outputs and may be shared. The input Uₘ is uniform on {0,1}ᵐ, and X is the law of f(Uₘ). There is no bound on m and no algorithmic uniformity requirement across n. For nonempty S⊆{0,…,n}, let U_Sⁿ be uniform on all strings x∈{0,1}ⁿ with |x|=Σⱼxⱼ∈S: every such string, rather than every allowed weight, has the same probability. For distributions P,Q on {0,1}ⁿ, TV(P,Q)=½Σₓ|P(x)−Q(x)|. The six comparison distributions are: a point mass at 0ⁿ; a point mass at 1ⁿ; equal mass on 0ⁿ and 1ⁿ; uniform on all even-weight strings; uniform on all odd-weight strings; and uniform on the entire cube. The quantifiers in the historical claim are ∃C>0 ∀d≥0 ∀ε∈(0,1) ∃n₀(d,ε) ∀n≥n₀ ∀m≥1 ∀d-local f ∀nonempty S: TV(f(Uₘ),U_Sⁿ)≤ε implies min_D TV(f(Uₘ),D)≤Cε, where D ranges over those six distributions. The result actually allows the threshold n₀ to depend only on d. No symmetry of f or of its output distribution is assumed.
cards.answer_criterion: The affirmative resolution is Theorem 4.1 of Kane, Ostuni and Wu, which proves the stated robust six-distribution classification, with an absolute multiplicative constant. Theorem 1.2 explicitly identifies this as the resolution of the Filmus–Leigh–Riazanov–Sokolov conjecture.

cards.title: Necessary logarithmic amplification when composing XOR with a total function
cards.formal: Historical existence question, resolved affirmatively: are there total nonconstant Boolean functions g for which the randomized query cost of XOR of n independent input blocks is Ω(n log n · R(g))? In explicit asymptotic terms, seek an absolute c>0 and, for arbitrarily large n, an input length m=m(n) and total nonconstant gₙ:{0,1}ᵐ→{0,1} with R(XORₙ∘gₙⁿ)≥c n log₂ n R(gₙ). The source also permits the analogous majority lower bound as an alternative affirmative answer. Corollary 1.3 of the 2023 paper establishes the XOR alternative. The inner function and its input length may grow with n; the claim is not about a single fixed finite truth table for unbounded n.
cards.why: Shows that error reduction can impose a genuine logarithmic cost in composing randomized computations even when every inner input is valid.
cards.status_note: Matched Open Question 12, including its truncated majority alternative, to the explicit total-function Corollary 1.3. cards.definitions: For input blocks x¹,…,xⁿ∈{0,1}ᵐ, (XORₙ∘gⁿ)(x¹,…,xⁿ)=g(x¹)⊕⋯⊕g(xⁿ), where ⊕ is addition modulo two. The blocks are separate parts of an arbitrary worst-case input; they are not promised to be randomly sampled. A randomized decision tree chooses which input bit to read next from previously read bits and internal random coins. Each bit read costs one query. R(h) is the smallest q for which such an algorithm always makes at most q queries, for every input and every coin outcome, and outputs h correctly with probability at least 2/3 on every input. There is no abort outcome and no postselection. Internal computation and the description of h are free; this is decision-tree complexity, denoted BPP(h) in the source, not the uniform time class BPP. Total means g is defined on all 2ᵐ inputs. The comparison uses the optimal cost of one copy, not the cost of a particular algorithm for g. In the source’s alternative, MAJₙ outputs one when at least n/2 of its input bits are one, including a tie. The later theorem also uses R̄δ(h): the minimum, over algorithms with error at most δ on every input, of the maximum over inputs of their expected query count. R̄ and R are distinct cost conventions; the stated resolved target uses R on both sides.
cards.answer_criterion: An unbounded family satisfying the displayed worst-case, 1/3-error lower bound for XOR answers the source question affirmatively; the generic O(n log n R(g)) upper bound makes the dependence tight up to constants. A majority family with the same lower bound would also answer the original disjunction, but is unnecessary once XOR is established. A promise function, noisy input oracle or postselection lower bound alone would not meet the total-function target.

cards.title: Grundy-value computation versus strategic determination
cards.formal:
Historical general-reduction question, answered negatively by the source under the explicit assumption \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{PSPACE}\): for every succinctly represented terminating impartial normal-play ruleset, can its Grundy value be computed by a deterministic polynomial-time procedure using strategic determination for that same ruleset as an oracle?

The source exhibits Undirected Geography as an obstruction. Its strategic determination is polynomial-time computable, whereas computing its Grundy value is PSPACE-hard, even on planar bipartite graphs of maximum degree four. Consequently, a general reduction of the stated kind would imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{PSPACE}\). This entry records that published conditional answer; it does not claim a proof that those complexity classes are different.

source_formulation.text: Is there a general polynomial-time reduction from Grundy-value computation to strategic determination?

cards.why: The result shows that an efficiently playable impartial game need not have an efficiently computable algebraic summary for interaction with other games. It separates the information needed to win a component from the information captured by its complete Sprague–Grundy value.

cards.definitions:
An impartial normal-play ruleset specifies positions and legal successor positions, with the same available moves for either player. The players alternate moves; a player with no legal move loses. Termination means that no play is infinite. A succinct representation encodes positions by finite binary strings, with a fixed algorithm enumerating their legal successors in time polynomial in the position’s encoding length. As in the source, all positions reachable from a position of length \(n\) have encoding length bounded by a fixed polynomial in \(n\). The ruleset and these algorithms are fixed, rather than part of each game input. The source’s obstruction already has a polynomial bound on play length.

The Grundy value is the nonnegative integer defined recursively by
\[
g(x)=\operatorname{mex}\{g(y):y\text{ is a legal successor of }x\},
\]
where \(\operatorname{mex}(S)=\min(\mathbb N_{0}\setminus S)\) and \(\operatorname{mex}(\varnothing)=0\). Termination and finite branching make the recursion well-founded. The value is at most the number of immediate legal successors, so its binary output is short in the stated representation. A position is losing exactly when its Grundy value is zero.

Strategic determination returns LOSING for a losing position; for a winning position it returns WINNING and one legal successor from which the next player loses. Thus it includes finding a winning move, not just deciding the winner.

The reduction under discussion is a deterministic polynomial-time Turing reduction, allowed polynomially many adaptive oracle calls on polynomial-length valid positions of the same fixed ruleset. Its ordinary computation, query writing and output are charged. The oracle must give correct strategic answers; any returned winning move is valid. A general reduction would have to work for every such ruleset. Even permitting a different polynomial-time reduction for each fixed ruleset cannot avoid the source’s obstruction unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{PSPACE}\). An oracle for a different, harder ruleset is outside this comparison.

In Undirected Geography, a position is an explicitly encoded finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) and a distinguished vertex \(s\) carrying a token. A move selects a neighbor \(t\) of \(s\), removes \(s\) and all its incident edges, and leaves the token at \(t\). A position with no neighbor at the token is terminal. Each move removes one vertex, so play lasts fewer than \(|V|\) moves. All graph positions are allowed. Restricting the hard instances to planar bipartite graphs with maximum degree four means that they can be drawn without crossings, their vertices split into two independent sets, and each vertex has at most four neighbors.

The class \(\mathrm P\) consists of decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time; \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\) uses polynomial working space. PSPACE-hardness of Grundy computation here means that exact computation would permit polynomial-time solutions of all PSPACE decision problems. The source in fact proves hardness of distinguishing particular small positive Grundy values. Hence this is a computational separation rather than an obstacle caused by writing a large integer.
cards.answer_criterion: The recorded answer is the conditional refutation: assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{PSPACE}\), the proposed general polynomial-time reduction does not exist. A ruleset with polynomial-time strategic determination but PSPACE-hard Grundy computation supplies the required obstruction, and the source proves that Undirected Geography has these properties. The assumption must remain part of the conclusion.

context_blocks.title: A positive value contains more information than winning
context_blocks.text: Knowing whether a Grundy value is zero determines whether the player to move can win. Determining which positive value occurs can be substantially harder. The source’s Undirected Geography theorem demonstrates this distinction even though finding winning moves is efficient.

context_blocks.title: The numerical summary has a separate role in sums
context_blocks.text: For the disjunctive sum of impartial games, a move changes exactly one component and the Grundy value of the sum is the bitwise XOR of component values. This explains why full Grundy information can be useful beyond winning an isolated component. The general-reduction question here concerns access to strategic determination for the original ruleset, not an oracle for arbitrary sums.
